title: Literacy Classrooms Where Ideas Matter
author: Michele Caracappa
summary: Michele Caracappa opens with Robert Caro's habit of fixing a book's theme, and even its last sentence, before he writes, and uses it to ask whether ideas matter in ELA classrooms. She returns to an SRI study finding that even in classrooms using materials labelled high quality, two-thirds of lessons produced only surface-level rather than robust comprehension. Robust comprehension means students build a complete mental model of the text that includes literal and inferential understanding, not just task completion. The study's list of effective practices helps only when those practices are oriented toward a big idea about the meaning of the whole text. Caracappa offers two moves: teacher teams should spend planning time discussing the meaning of the text itself rather than atomizing lessons into parts, and teachers should give ideas more airtime in discussion. In particular, she suggests pausing on the quality of a student's claim before asking for evidence, so that citing evidence serves meaningful interpretation rather than becoming a habit for its own sake.
points: The SRI finding that two-thirds of lessons in high-quality materials still stay surface-level shows that good curriculum does not guarantee deep comprehension.
Robust comprehension depends on students building a complete mental model of the text, which requires the teacher to hold one first.
Instructional practices such as questioning and evidence-citing only produce robust work when they serve a big idea about the meaning of the whole text.
Teacher planning protocols often break lessons into parts, so teams should first spend time discussing and dissecting the meaning of the text itself.
Before asking students for evidence, teachers should examine the sophistication of the claim, since evidence-citing without a meaningful claim thins out the thinking.
quotes: What’s exciting to me about the book is the extent to which, from its opening pages, the book is alive with ideas about its subject – or, its dual subjects: the “power broker” himself Robert Moses and the city he shaped.

That study found that even in classrooms leveraging materials labeled as “high-quality instructional materials,” two-thirds of lessons only facilitated “surface-level” rather than “robust” understanding of texts.

Merely implementing these practices, however, will not necessarily lead to lessons that feature robust comprehension work. To do so, the practices must be oriented toward a big idea about a meaning of the whole text.
After all, if we want students to develop a mental model of the text as a whole, we must be operating from one ourselves.
Many protocols for teacher planning and preparation, however, atomize lessons into disparate parts.
But in implementation, I often see an over-emphasis on teaching the habit of citing evidence and an under-emphasis on evidence in service of making a meaningful claim about the text.
If we always jump straight to “what’s your evidence” and don’t spend time appreciating and refining the claim itself, we risk losing the depth of our meaning making.
If we want our ELA classes to spaces where students truly savor what they’re reading, we’ve got to make space to center the ideas of the text.
